item.description: arXiv:2611.32138v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In embedding-based video anomaly detection (VAD), normal clips can have high similarity to anomalous descriptions, an anomaly bias that leads to false positives. Methods such as PRISM mitigate this bias by measuring deviations from a normality reference along anomaly directions. Both the normality reference and the anomaly directions are derived from text and shared across videos, although normal activity and the appearance of anomalies vary across scenes. The resulting scores are also sensitive to prompt selection. To address these limitations, we propose Visual Intrinsic Distribution Estimation (VIDE), a training-free framework that adapts text-derived scoring to each test video using frozen clip embeddings. VIDE estimates normal scene content from clips with low initial anomaly scores and uses this estimate to partially correct the textual reference. It then rescales category responses, penalizes clips with strong responses across categories, and refines the anomaly directions using high-scoring clips. VIDE averages scores across prompt views to reduce sensitivity to prompt selection and fuses scores from two frozen encoders. With both encoders, VIDE improves AUC over the best PRISM result by $1.5$, $1.9$, and $3.5$ points on UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, respectively, and AP by $6.5$ points on XD-Violence and $9.3$ points on MSAD. VIDE yields the highest AUC among the compared training-free methods on all three benchmarks and the highest reported AUC among all compared methods on XD-Violence and MSAD. Our code is included in the supplementary material and will be made publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Kevin D. Nguetche, Atif Belal, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli

item.title: ARS-VLM: Visually Aligned Augmented Random Search for Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.32147v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.
item.dc:creator: Xiangwei Wang, Jianyuan Lin, Peng Wang, Saman Halgamuge

item.title: Beyond Autoregression: Diffusion Language Model is All Analog In-Memory Computing Need
item.description: arXiv:2611.32223v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) enables energy-efficient language-model inference, but hardware non-idealities perturb matrix--vector multiplications and degrade generation quality. Autoregressive (AR) models are especially vulnerable: each token is committed to the causal context at birth, so perturbation-induced errors cascade. We study diffusion language models (DLMs), which iteratively refine a masked sequence, as an alternative paradigm. Across scale-matched model pairs and open checkpoints, DLMs degrade more gracefully than AR counterparts under persistent weight perturbations. Controlled analyses rule out cross-round noise averaging and support delayed token commitment and progressive context resolution as the mechanism. A larger denoising-step budget further shrinks the clean--noisy gap, a DLM-specific latency--robustness knob. We perform large-scale simulation tests across diverse datasets and models using a noise model calibrated from real silicon measurements. Furthermore, on a 16-chip 28nm eFlash AIMC cluster, hybrid on-board measurements show DLMs tolerate $1.4$--$3\times$ larger weight noise, making diffusion-based generation a promising paradigm for noise-resilient AIMC inference.
item.dc:creator: Yuanuo Feng, Yubing Ye, Yizhe Chen, Wenshuai Yao, Ngai Wong, Wenyong Zhou, Wang Kang

item.title: Relational Bottleneck Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.32227v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Achieving both interpretable and high-performance inference is a key challenge in deep learning. While Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) provide inherent interpretability, they are constrained by task-specific training and rely on isolated visual concepts that fail to capture higher-order visual semantic relationships. Conversely, Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate zero-shot capabilities through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, standard CoT lacks a strict causal dependency between the generated rationale and the final output, compromising faithfulness. To bridge this gap, we propose Relational Bottleneck Models (RBMs), a novel training-free framework that transforms any off-the-shelf LVLMs into inherently interpretable models in a plug-and-play manner. RBMs consist of two stages: (i) Structured Rationale Generation (SRG), which explicitly models semantic interactions between visual concepts as subject-predicate-object triplets, and (ii) Rationale-Grounded Decoding (RGD), which enforces a strict causal dependency between the rationales and the final output. RGD aggregates rationale-conditional next-token distributions via an importance-weighted product-of-experts strategy, strictly excluding the image inputs from the decoding context. Extensive zero-shot evaluations across diverse benchmarks and LVLM backbones demonstrate that RBMs achieve superior interpretability while improving task performance over CBM baselines, entirely without task-specific fine-tuning.
item.dc:creator: Shin'ya Yamaguchi, Kosuke Nishida

item.title: MYSTIQUE: Few-Shot Facial Identity Transfer with Performance Preservation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32232v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In visual effects, identity transfer replaces the identity in a driving image with that of a target person, while preserving the expression, lighting, pose and scene of that image. Paired ground truth is rarely available, so many methods are trained by self-reconstruction, where the model can learn a shortcut by copying identity cues from the driving image. This shortcut causes identity leakage at inference, where the driving image shows a different person. Our key observation is that leakage can enter through any input that reads the driving image. We therefore present MYSTIQUE, a diffusion-based identity transfer method that takes identity from a set of the target's photos and reads expression, lighting and scene through separate streams. It learns to disentangle identity from the other streams through multi-stage training, with disentanglement strategies at their inputs: a random block mask whose boundaries do not follow the face outline, self-augmentation, which randomly changes the face shape in the expression input and keeps its expression, and face randomization, which replaces the person in the expression and lighting inputs while the ground truth stays the driving image. At inference, we also warp the lighting input onto the face shape of a first pass, which reduces face-shape leakage through the lighting stream. Since face-recognition scores and human judgments each have limits, we evaluate identity with both, together with face-shape metrics on rendered faces of known shape. In a user study, raters judge MYSTIQUE's results more like the target than those of each compared method. Among these methods, MYSTIQUE also recovers the target's face shape most accurately, and its recognition score gains the most as more photos of the target are given.
item.dc:creator: Shihan Cheng, David Hyde, Junting Deng, Michael Bao, Paul Debevec, Roshni Cooper, Soshi Shimada

item.title: $\epsilon$-Seg++: Ensembling Across Hierarchy and Training Time for Label-Efficient EM Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic segmentation of electron microscopy (EM) volumes is a central step in quantitative cell biology, but dense voxel-wise annotation is prohibitively expensive. $\epsilon$-Seg showed that a hierarchical variational autoencoder trained on sparsely annotated voxels can yield competitive segmentations, but it classifies from its topmost latent level only and operates exclusively on 2D patches. We introduce $\epsilon$-Seg++, which places a semantic expert at every level of the hierarchy and consolidates their predictions with a parameter-free product of experts. We further enable 3D inputs through a leakage-free sub-volume splitting protocol, which allows 2D and 3D models to be compared under identical sparse supervision. Because validation labels are just as scarce as training labels, we treat checkpoint selection as part of the method and average the top-ranked checkpoints, a second ensemble, this time across training time. On the BetaSeg FIB-SEM dataset, the multi-level experts improve 2D mean Dice by about 0.1 at 2,500 training labels. With up to 600 training labels, the 2D model matches or exceeds 3D $\epsilon$-Seg at about one eleventh of its prediction cost. Above roughly a thousand labels, 3D inputs dominate, and at matched annotation cost 3D $\epsilon$-Seg++ reaches a mean Dice of 0.905 versus 0.880 for D3PM, while predicting between 5.4 and 27 times faster (with our checkpoint ensemble or a single model, respectively). Checkpoint ensembling matches single-best selection on average and markedly improves the worst case when the validation set is small.
item.dc:creator: Edoardo Giacomello, Sheida Rahnamai Kordasiabi, Mehdi Seifi, Florian Jug

item.title: ASTERISM: Do Multimodal LLMs Actually Look at All the Images?
item.description: arXiv:2611.32316v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.
item.dc:creator: Chanseul Cho, Dongwoo Kim, Noori Bae, Seungjae Moon, Seongsu Lee, Youngmin Ro

item.title: A Description-Derived Drug-Drug Interaction Benchmark Reveals Split-Dependent Molecular Representation Rankings
item.description: arXiv:2611.32371v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction is clinically important and poses a distinct challenge for molecular representation learning. Unlike single-molecule property prediction, DDI requires a predictor to compose two molecular representations into a relational outcome. DrugBank provides curator-authored DDI descriptions rather than ready-made categorical labels, so a categorical prediction target must first be derived from the text. We construct a dataset of DDI pairs by mapping processed descriptions to six text-derived categories and define a benchmark with four holdout regimes that restrict train-test chemical overlap from random pairs to scaffold-disjoint evaluation. We then use this benchmark to compare molecular fingerprints, pretrained sequence representations, and graph-derived features across five seeds and multiple classifier heads. Molecular fingerprints lead the high- overlap random split, whereas graph-derived representations lead the drug- and scaffold-holdout regimes, with the gap increasing as molecular overlap is restricted. Changing the classifier head affects absolute performance but not the relative representation ranking. These results show that representation rankings change with test-set novelty under a fixed description-derived label space.
item.dc:creator: Manel Gil-Sorribes, Isaac Filella-Merce, Alexis Molina

item.title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
item.description: arXiv:2611.32384v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.
item.dc:creator: Songtao Jiang, Yuan Wang, Fucheng Niu, Hualiang Wang, Jian Wu, Zuozhu Liu

item.title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories
item.description: arXiv:2611.32391v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.
item.dc:creator: Philom\`ene Letzelter, Violaine Courrier, Sandrine Katsahian, Agathe Guilloux

item.title: Analysis of Federated Graph Neural Networks for Predicting Nuclear Core Properties
item.description: arXiv:2611.32509v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated learning has grown in popularity owing to the increasing data privacy and safety concerns. It allows multiple parties to collaboratively train a model without exchanging their raw data. As an example of highly sensitive infrastructure of national importance, nuclear reactors benefit from this approach, where---while pooling multiple large datasets from different institutions could improve machine learning solutions---the confidentiality of the datasets is paramount. In this paper, we demonstrate that a graph neural network (GNN) outperforms the convolutional neural network (CNN) baseline in a federated setting for a use case concerning nuclear reactor core optimization. The GNN architecture is better suited for the nuclear reactor geometry as, unlike the CNN, it does not require padding the cylindrical core and does not assume translation invariance. The key finding of this work is that input representation is more important than model size and complexity. More sophisticated federated algorithms were employed, but the improvements derived were of lower magnitude. Experimenting with training corpus volume led to the discovery that greater fuel inventory variance is more beneficial than arrangements of existing cases, which is a direct consequence of data heterogeneity. Going forward, focus will remain on enhancing the input and readout representation.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Ko\v{z}ul, Mihailo Ili\'c, Julia Bartos, Tuan Tran, Milo\v{s} Savi\'c, Vladimir Kurbalija, Edo Frederix, Du\v{s}an Jakoveti\'c

item.title: Advanced Synthetic Image Detection Using Hybrid Feature Extraction
item.description: arXiv:2611.32538v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the realm of generative AI, models such as GANs, MidJourney, DALL-E, and others have been continuously evolving to generate increasingly lifelike images. This rapid advancement has created an urgent need for robust methods to distinguish between real and AI-generated images. This paper proposes a novel approach for the detection of synthetic images by employing deep learning techniques for feature analysis. The proposed architecture classifies images by identifying variations that generative models struggle to replicate, particularly fine-grained textures and complex object features. Deformations in complexes are examined with the help of the CBAM architecture along with ResNet50. We have performed a selective patch-based analysis using Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) scoring, extracting the regions with the most and least complexity for further processing with an SRM Module and ResNet50 module. Experimental results show that our approach achieves high accuracy in classifying real-world images from synthetic ones, contributing to the development of more reliable detection frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Ameya Uppina, S Navaneetha Krishnan, Nikhil N Iyer, Joe Dhanith P R

item.title: Breaking Routing And Inter-device Dependencies in Mixture-of-Experts
item.description: arXiv:2611.32572v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale, Expert Parallelism (EP) becomes increasingly important for distributing experts across devices. However, the resulting token dispatch and combine operations can become a major bottleneck during inference. Overlapping these communication phases with computation is constrained by the sequential dependencies of standard MoE architectures. We introduce BRAID-MoE, an architecture that pairs laddered residual connections with early routing to relax these dependencies. Laddered residuals enable each expert combine to be deferred to the following block, while early routing computes the next routing decision from the pre-combine residual, with experts still receiving the updated post-combine hidden state. This creates an extended communication window in which the preceding combine and next dispatch can execute back-to-back on a dedicated communication stream, overlapping attention computation. On Qwen3-shaped MoEs with 0.4B-A0.1B and 2.5B-A0.5B parameters, BRAID closely matches sequential training at matched compute, with validation-loss increases of only 1% and 0.5%, respectively. We further demonstrate that existing MoE checkpoints can be adapted to BRAID with limited additional training, largely recovering their original accuracy. On a converted Qwen3-30B-A3B model, BRAID achieves speedups of up to 1.29$\times$ in prefill and 1.37$\times$ in decode, and at least 1.12$\times$ across diverse workloads and EP configurations on one or two four-H100 nodes. It outperforms competing overlap strategies in all tested settings, with the strongest gains when communication is a major latency bottleneck and its duration approaches the available computation window. These results demonstrate that early routing enables more effective communication-computation overlap in MoE inference at a modest cost in model quality.
item.dc:creator: John Zarka (MLIA), Danyal Ahmed (MLIA), Eugene Belilovsky (DIRO, MILA), Edouard Oyallon (MLIA)

item.title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
item.description: arXiv:2611.32595v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that the following problem is \textbf{NEXPTIME}-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.
item.dc:creator: Marco S\"alzer

item.title: OpenWoud: Vendor-Unlocked Scalable Adaptive Random Forest Accelerator
item.description: arXiv:2611.32662v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online Machine Learning (ML) enables real-time decision-making on evolving data streams. These dynamic models learn continuously to adapt to new concepts, as previous ones become invalid, but their performance is often limited by throughput. The Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) is a state-of-the-art model for this setting, which naturally exposes parallelism and is therefore well-suited for hardware acceleration. However, prior Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based accelerators are vendor-locked and rely on resource-hungry Floating-Point (FP) arithmetics, limiting their scalability and portability. We present OpenWoud, a vendor-unlocked ARF framework for FPGAs. Our design replaces FP operators with a flexible FiXed-Point (FxP) arithmetic library and introduces fully transparent, manually scheduled dataflows for training and drift detection. This enables fine-grained time/area trade-offs and predictable behavior across platforms. A comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real datasets shows that OpenWoud maintains or increases accuracy (up to +12.89%), compared to a prior FPGA accelerator, while reducing the resource utilization by half. Competitive performance is observed compared to GPU (0.5 - 1.5x speed-up) and an FPGA baseline (0.2 - 0.5x), despite the latter being based on idealized simulation. Crucially, OpenWoud sustains true sample-by-sample inference, unlike GPUs that require batch insertion.
item.dc:creator: Ewout van Nimwegen, Elijah Seth Cishugi, Hendrik Folmer, Marco Ottavi, Kuan-Hsun Chen

item.title: A Hybrid Analytical-Neural Residual Surrogate for Fast Radio Propagation Prediction over Irregular Terrain
item.description: arXiv:2611.32698v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fast prediction of radio-wave propagation over irregular terrain is important for coverage analysis in mountainous environments, where many terrain and antenna configurations must be evaluated repeatedly. High-fidelity split-step parabolic equation (SSPE) solvers can capture terrain-induced shadowing and interference, but their computational cost is high for repeated planning studies. Learning-based surrogates reduce this cost, but direct field regression asks the network to learn both analytically tractable propagation trends and terrain-dependent residual structure. This paper proposes a hybrid analytical-neural residual surrogate that separates these two parts. A deterministic analytical baseline represents free-space spreading, antenna directivity, modified knife-edge diffraction, and terrain-aware specular reflection, while a compact coarse-to-fine neural network predicts the residual field. The network uses baseline-derived guidance channels, anisotropic convolutions, and feature-wise antenna conditioning to match the directional structure of terrain propagation fields. On synthetic SSPE data at 1.0 GHz, the proposed model achieves an MAE of 2.1061 dB, compared with 3.3955 dB for a standard U-Net and 3.2560 dB for a reproduced physics-guided CNN, while reducing the average inference time to 11.30 ms per sample. A zero-shot test at 1.8 GHz gives an MAE of 2.8692 dB without retraining, and a case study on the measured Hjorringvej terrain profile shows that the prediction remains consistent with the SSPE reference and follows the measured path-loss trend.
item.dc:creator: Yongyuan Hu, Jiahao Li, Keqi Ni, Yuqi Ouyang, Hao Qin

item.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32718v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
item.dc:creator: Itai Mizlish, Boaz Ben-Moshe

item.title: Quantum Community Detection for Data Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.32738v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Community detection offers an alternative to conventional methods for data analysis tasks such as feature selection and clustering, and detecting communities with quantum algorithms is a promising avenue for quantum speedup. We investigate quantum spectral community detectors, such as the modularity-matrix algorithm deteQt, in pipelines for both tasks. We first generalise deteQt to multiple communities by recursive bisection, and show that it recovers planted communities, and hence redundant features, in synthetic and small datasets. We then propose projeQt, which applies a spectral filter to the encoded modularity matrix through the quantum singular value transformation, retaining higher-order eigenvectors that deteQt does not use. projeQt acts on the generalised modularity matrix and extracts several communities at once, without recursion, by k-means clustering of a Gram matrix built from quantum state overlaps. On MNIST we demonstrate both pipelines, selecting informative pixels and classifying images directly by clustering, and find them competitive with standard community detectors.
item.dc:creator: Vicente P. Soloviev, Brian Coyle, Stefano Scali, Michal Krompiec

item.title: NCPU: Towards Cell-Inspired Spatial Computing
item.description: arXiv:2611.32750v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simple cellular automata (CAs) can be computationally universal, but their rules are designed by hand. We train Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs), which learn a local update rule by gradient descent, to compute exact digital logic. Bits are encoded as clusters of cells on a 2D grid, and a result reaches the output only by propagating through intermediate cells. One model is trained per task: logic gates, 4- and 8-bit ripple-carry adders, and a preliminary 8-bit arithmetic logic unit (ALU). All gate and adder models reach 100% bit correctness in 10 of 10 seeds, and exhaustive tests over all input pairs find at most 1 error in 256 (4-bit) and 7 in 65,536 (8-bit). Adders trained on operands of up to 3 bits generalize to 8 bits. The adders propagate the carry as a wave, with a delay of about 3.5 steps per bit of the carry chain. Outputs are correct only within the trained rollout length.
item.dc:creator: Iliya Zhechev, Piotr Walas

item.title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.32755v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.
item.dc:creator: Wonjune Seo, Minkyung Park, Saerom Park

item.title: NABLA: A Noise-Adaptive Blockwise Left-Right Preconditioning Algorithm for Stochastic Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.32781v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose NABLA, a noise-adaptive blockwise left-right preconditioning algorithm for mini-batch stochastic nonconvex optimization. NABLA combines an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients with block-diagonal row and column preconditioners constructed from matrix-valued second-moment statistics. Unlike conventional matrix-preconditioned methods that use fixed decay parameters, NABLA adjusts the second-moment averaging coefficient through a closed-loop feedback rule determined by the cumulative stochastic-gradient energy and its running average. The first-moment coefficient remains fixed, allowing the trajectory-dependent adaptation to act directly on the structured preconditioners. The resulting method is horizon-free, requires no prior knowledge of the noise level, and automatically adjusts the memory of its second-moment estimators to the observed optimization dynamics. Under standard lower boundedness, smoothness, unbiasedness, bounded-variance, and spectral-boundedness assumptions, we establish uniform stability and variation bounds for the time-varying block preconditioners and control their interaction with momentum estimation and parameter updates. These results yield the noise-adaptive stationarity guarantee $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2}+\sigma^{1/2}T^{-1/4})$, which automatically reduces to the nearly deterministic $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ rate when the stochastic-gradient noise vanishes. NABLA therefore provides a principled approach to combining closed-loop trajectory feedback with memory-efficient structured matrix preconditioning.
item.dc:creator: Yanlin Li, Ganzhao Yuan

item.title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32786v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
item.dc:creator: Tingting Liao, Mingjia Huo, Hao Li, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu

item.title: Data-driven Reduced-order Modeling of a Multistable Viscoelastic Flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.32818v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Viscoelastic flow past two side-by-side microcylinders has been shown to exhibit geometry-dependent transitions among symmetric, converging, diverging, and asymmetric-diverging flow states, together with regions of bistability and tristability. Here, we develop a data-driven framework for learning a two-dimensional, parameter-dependent normal form for this bifurcation structure from sparse measurements of stable flow states. We use the flow asymmetry parameters $I'$ and $I''$ as state variables, with the gap ratio $G$ and Weissenberg number $Wi$ as control parameters. In the absence of trajectory data, the measured steady states are enforced as stable equilibria of the learned vector field through equilibrium and local-stability constraints. We examine both polynomial and neural-network representations of the associated normal form and incorporate the physical reflection symmetry directly into the model. The resulting models recover the main geometry-dependent transitions and the overall structure of the experimental phase diagram. To reduce additional stable equilibria that are not constrained by the measurements, we introduce an iterative negative-sample procedure that refines the predicted equilibrium structure. Combining equilibrium data, local stability, physical symmetry, and negative samples yields the closest agreement with the experimental phase diagram among the models considered. The remaining discrepancies reflect the limited information available, solely in the form of sparse equilibrium measurements. Overall, the framework aims to showcase a prototypical example of both the potential and the limitations of inferring nonlinear flow dynamics from sparse equilibrium measurements and highlight the importance of physical constraints and additional dynamical information for reconstructing complex bifurcation structures.
item.dc:creator: Shaoxuan Chen, Su Yang, Simon J. Haward, Amy Q. Shen, Panayotis G. Kevrekidis

item.title: Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables
item.description: arXiv:2611.32851v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure methods used to generate their training data, and refining them against experimental measurements provides a direct route beyond this limit. However, such refinement remains difficult for dynamical observables because differentiating chaotic molecular trajectories yields unstable gradients. Here, we introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories themselves. The resulting gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as the trajectory length increases. We validated the gradient estimator against finite-difference calculations and used it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves the predictions of shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which is included in the optimization objective. Alignment at a single temperature also improves the apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing their temperature dependences closer to experiments. Moreover, the optimized potential exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent, higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating that alignment with experiments improves the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets. PathGrad thus establishes a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force field optimizations.
item.dc:creator: Zhongyao Wang, Lun Song, Yakun Zeng, Xingao Gong, Rui Shi, Mao Su

item.title: What Does a Skill Vocabulary Cost? A Closed-Loop Decomposition over Demonstrated Motions
item.description: arXiv:2611.32858v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Xiling Li, Nils Blank, Paul Mattes, Pankhuri Vanjani, Rudolf Lioutikov

item.title: Label leakage through file headers: geometry and batch confounds in public mammography datasets, and a pre-training acceptance gate
item.description: arXiv:2611.32899v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A dataset whose diagnostic label can be recovered from non-diagnostic information yields high, reproducible and uninformative model performance. We applied pre-training controls that see only image geometry, global texture, a sub-collection identifier or one covariate to six public mammography datasets, against a stop threshold of AUC 0.60. In KAU-BCMD, geometry alone predicted the BI-RADS class at AUC 1.0000 in a local copy and at a mean of 0.979 in a public Kaggle archive; after resizing, texture alone gave 0.847. In CMMD, the sub-collection prefix predicted malignancy at 0.7753; the restricted sub-collection passed geometry (0.5000) and texture (0.5810) but failed an identifier-order control added post hoc (test AUC 0.9926). CBIS-DDSM exceeded the stop on geometry (pooled mean 0.654 over 20 splits), a verdict statistic chosen post hoc; its official mass and calcification splits did not. M-SYNTH, INbreast and a partial VinDr-Mammo copy passed the few controls run. We release the code and derived tables. There is no quantum component in the inference path.
item.dc:creator: Achraf Toufah, Rana Saad, Moulay Youssef El Hafidi

item.title: Theory-Informed Quantum Error Mitigation for Shor Order Finding with Fourier Neural Operators
item.description: arXiv:2611.32923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum noise distorts the distribution of circuit measurement outcomes, often leaving enough information to infer the algorithm's correct result. To recover this latent information from the noisy distribution in Shor order finding, we introduce a theory-informed quantum error mitigation method. We model how circuit errors shift, broaden, or weaken peaks in the output distribution. These models guide both the generation of synthetic training data and the design of a Fourier neural operator with a learned gain that attenuates or amplifies higher retained Fourier modes. We score each candidate order by averaging the correlations between its ideal distribution and the distributions measured in three circuit executions. The network adjusts these scores to guide the order estimate and determine the weights of a normalized mixture of the ideal distributions. On 1,351 simulated test cases for general modular exponentiation, held out by circuit configuration, exact order recovery rises from 19% to 34%, and the median Jensen-Shannon divergence from the ideal distribution falls by 50%, from 0.64 to 0.32. On 101 Mersenne rotation circuits executed across five IBM quantum processors, a separate model trained and calibrated in simulation increases the number of correct order estimates from 35 to 53. Algorithmic structure can remain recoverable even when noise makes it barely visible.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Markidis, Qingxin Yang, Erik {\AA}sgrim, Ivy Peng

item.title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
item.dc:creator: Ayush Barik, Fan Lai, Francis Y. Yan

item.title: Quantum kernels on breast data: concentration, surrogates, and two ways an advantage gets manufactured
item.description: arXiv:2611.32942v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum-kernel advantage claims on breast data are usually a single number: one quantum arm, one comparator, one test split. We asked what that number measures once the full comparator set and selection history are visible. We report three active benchmarks, all exact classical statevector simulations of 8-qubit fidelity kernels with no quantum component in the inference path: a sample-efficiency sweep on Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer at ten training-set sizes; raw-versus-processed arms on 1,200 M-SYNTH simulated mammograms with a matched closed-form dequantisation surrogate, five classical methods at the same input and eleven kernel families; and a 30-seed selection-inflation measurement on BreastMNIST. A CMMD D1 clinical arm is withdrawn as a result arm because its frozen splits leak the label through patient serial order, a defect reported in a separate study; it is retained only as a worked example. All three active arms are negative. On M-SYNTH raw an apparent +0.1736 (p = 5.2e-06) against a tuned RBF-SVM falls to +0.0019 (p = 0.937) against a random forest at the same input, and a Laplacian kernel wins on validation. On WDBC, with model selection confined to training data, the quantum kernel is below the selected classical arm at every training-set size, with 2 of 200 paired subsamples ahead. Best-of-30 seed selection adds +0.0210 on BreastMNIST. One result does not fit: at bandwidth 2pi the matched closed-form Gaussian surrogate failed to reproduce the M-SYNTH raw kernel (0.5410 against 0.7045, p = 6.3e-06). Comparator choice and selection each produce effects larger than any quantum-classical difference we measured; we give a reporting standard that removes both.
item.dc:creator: Rana Saad, Achraf Toufah, Moulay Youssef El Hafidi

item.title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.32945v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clustering is a foundational tool for exploratory data analysis across the sciences. We argue that clustering methods should be evaluated along four dimensions: fidelity to the data's underlying structure, interpretability of the recovered groups, stability under data perturbations and algorithmic randomness, and scalability to modern scientific datasets. Yet existing methods rarely satisfy all four criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PHM-ensemble, a general probabilistic framework for multiresolution clustering that estimates the underlying data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits and subsequently constructs a clustering hierarchy through hierarchical merging of the mixture components. On simulated datasets and the MNIST benchmark, PHM-ensemble matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms in agreement with ground truth, produces more stable results across runs, and reveals complex underlying structures. Applied to 1.82 million peripheral blood cells from the Human Immune Health Atlas, PHM-ensemble achieves higher agreement with expert-curated major cell-type annotations than the Leiden clustering used in the original study (adjusted Rand index 0.965 versus 0.789), while requiring only half the computing time. Beyond identifying major immune lineages, it reveals biologically coherent relationships among cell types and resolves finer structure within individual lineages, uncovering subtypes and cellular states consistent with known biology.
item.dc:creator: Ali Turfah, Xiaoquan Wen

item.title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.32947v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch's treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.
item.dc:creator: Aniruddhan Ganesaraman, Michael R. Kosorok

item.title: Train What You Run: Probabilistic Convolutions for Learning Token Compaction in State Space Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33009v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual token compaction reduces inference cost by passing only selected image patches or video tokens to later layers. In sequence models with local convolutions, each removal changes which tokens are neighbors. Learning which tokens to keep therefore requires a training signal that accounts for the new neighborhoods. We introduce ProbConv, which computes the exact expected convolution before activation at a kept position under independent keep decisions. The operator is differentiable in the keep probabilities. With binary decisions, ProbConv and step gating reproduce the compacted Mamba block. Across image, vision--language and video backbones, ProbConv is strongest under strong compaction: its advantage over matched training controls grows as more tokens are removed. In Cobra, it also outperforms adaptations of published vision--language pruning methods at matched inference budgets. ProbConv also improves over matched zero-mask training in video frame selection and speech frame dropping. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gmum/probconv
item.dc:creator: Piotr Kubaty (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland, Doctoral School of Exact and Natural Sciences, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland), Mikhail Saladkou (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland), Jacek Tabor (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland, Centre for Credible Artificial Intelligence, Warsaw University of Technology, Poland), {\L}ukasz Struski (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland)

item.title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.33036v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu, Sipeng Chen, Weikai Li, Tianyi Chen, Qiancheng Yang, Hang Zhou, Yizhou Sun, Wei Wang, Xiao Luo

item.title: Auditing the Judge: Human-Derived Bias Discovery, Quantification, and Mitigation in LLM Judges
item.description: arXiv:2611.33065v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators in evaluation and training pipelines, their judgements are often affected by systematic biases that conflict with human preferences. Although prior work has identified various biases and proposed methods for detecting and mitigating them, less attention has been paid to using human preferences to inform bias identification and mitigation. Moreover, these approaches rely heavily on pre-discovered bias lists, overlook bias strength, and depend on costly interventions. In this work, we propose HUB-J, an integrated framework based on human-derived bias factors that detects, quantifies, and mitigates biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Our approach leverages human-LLM judgement disagreement cases to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, and utilizes agreement cases to quantify bias strength through controlled input modifications and resulting shifts in model decisions. Finally, building on these quantified biases, we introduce a lightweight, training-free regression-based mitigation strategy that estimates the influence of each bias factor on model judgments and corrects bias-influenced decisions by removing its estimated effect. Empirical results show that HUB-J uncovers both known and novel bias factors, reveals meaningful differences in model susceptibility, and consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models.
item.dc:creator: Hamin Koo, Chanjoo Jung, Fangzhao Wu, Jaehyung Kim

item.title: The Reliability Function of Error-Correcting Output Codes with Noisy Binary Classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2611.33068v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Error-correcting output coding (ECOC) builds a multi-class classifier from binary classifiers. We study the excess error rate of ECOC over the Bayes (MAP) classifier when each binary classifier outputs a posterior estimate whose log-odds is corrupted by Gaussian noise. Recasting decoding as a test over a Gaussian channel, we derive an upper bound from the union and Chernoff bounds and a lower bound from the nearest competing category and the Mills ratio. The bounds show that a large Hamming distance is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the excess error rate. The excess error rate stays bounded away from zero, by a constant that depends on the two largest posteriors and the noise level but not on the number of categories $M$, whenever the distance between the code words of the two most probable categories is bounded; for equidistant codes this distance is $d_{\min}$. Conversely, it is at most $M-1$ times a factor that is exponentially small in the minimum distance $d_{\min}$, and it vanishes whenever $\kappa\,d_{\min}-\ln(M-1)\to\infty$ for an explicit $\kappa$ (for general codes, under a posterior condition). For $n$-vs-rest codes with $n\geq2$, the upper and lower exponents coincide asymptotically, which determines the reliability function of ECOC in closed form. The results extend to correlated Gaussian noise with the Hamming distance replaced by an effective distance; when noise is shared at the level of categories, the effective distance stays bounded and the excess error rate does not vanish for any code. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. In a semi-synthetic setting, the measured decay agrees with the predicted exponent. On ResNet-50 features of CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k, the excess error over a log-likelihood decoding reference decreases with $d_{\min}$ and, for larger $M$, levels off at a moderate distance, while codes with $d_{\min}=1$ degrade as $M$ grows.
item.dc:creator: Gendo Kumoi, Hideki Yagi, Manabu Kobayashi, Shigeichi Hirasawa

item.title: The Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) Dataset
item.description: arXiv:2611.33088v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Monitoring Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) supports safety and well-being for people living at home, especially older adults, and radar sensing is gaining increasing attention in the field of activity recognition for its ability to ensure privacy in the home while also surpassing technical limitations of other sensing modalities. However, radar-based activity recognition remains constrained by the limited availability of large-scale datasets. We introduce the Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) dataset to addresses the gaps identified in existing work: 1) it expands the scale of available data by providing over eight hours of annotated recordings in which a person performs eight distinct activities; 2) it overcomes room configuration limitations by recording from five different locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment; and 3) it extends beyond primitive actions to focus on high-level ADLs. In addition to the dataset, this paper introduces practical guidance for future ADL dataset construction. We conducted a detailed analysis of how ADLs are prioritized across academic research, health survey tools, and clinical trials to identify clinically significant ADLs. Furthermore, we provide our experimental design, data collection and annotation strategies, post-processing pipeline for forming the R-ADL dataset from raw data, and baseline results on standard machine learning architectures. The R-ADL dataset serves as a valuable resource for advancing ADL recognition systems as we continue building larger and more diverse datasets.
item.dc:creator: Dominique Regli, Brian C. Williams

item.title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
item.description: arXiv:2611.33130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $\beta$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.
item.dc:creator: Kshitiz, Zheyuan Hu, Robyn Wu, Yizhou Li, Yunchu Zhang, Vattanary Tevy, Kavya Tayal, Shawn Yin, Aykut Onol, Kushal Arora, Dhruv Shah, Abhishek Gupta, Zackory Erickson, Aviral Kumar

item.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.33141v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.
item.dc:creator: Vansh Kapoor, Max Sobol Mark, Sreyas Venkataraman, Max Simchowitz, Aviral Kumar

item.title: BioLoom: Scaling Biomedical Vision-Language Models by Learning from the Structure of Scientific Articles
item.description: arXiv:2611.33151v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.
item.dc:creator: Yuwei Yang, Xiaoxiao Sun, Alejandro Lozano, Yuan-Sen Ting, Yuhui Yuan, Liang Zheng, Serena Yeung-Levy

item.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
item.description: arXiv:2611.33158v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/
item.dc:creator: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Jiayuan Yan, Bohan Fang, Wisdom Oluchi Ikezogwo, Ainaz Eftekhar, Max Argus, Jason Ren, Jiafei Duan, Ranjay Krishna

item.title: Solving Attention Kernel Regression Problem via Pre-conditioner
item.description: arXiv:2308.14304v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The attention mechanism is the key to large language models, and the attention matrix serves as an algorithmic and computational bottleneck for such a scheme. In this paper, we define two problems, motivated by designing fast algorithms for proxy of attention matrix and solving regressions against them. Given an input matrix $A\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and a response vector $b$, the first proxy, for $n\gg d$, uses powers of the matrix $A^\top A$, and we consider two types of regression problems: $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}\|(A^\top A)^jx-b\|_2$ and $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}\|A(A^\top A)^jx-b\|_2$ for any positive integer $j$. We design fast algorithms for these power regressions, based on sketching and preconditioning. The second proxy is applying exponential entrywise to the Gram matrix, denoted by $\exp(AA^\top)$ and solving the regression $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^n}\|\exp(AA^\top)x-b \|_2$. We call this problem the attention kernel regression problem, as the matrix $\exp(AA^\top)$ could be viewed as a kernel function with respect to $A$. For this problem, we show that the sketching and preconditioning approach known for Gaussian kernels gives error $\epsilon\|b\|_2$ for every $b$, with a sketch dimension that is, up to logarithmic factors, $\epsilon^{-2}n$ times the condition number of the kernel matrix, which is at least $n/e$ when the rows of $A$ have norm at most $1$. For rows of norm at most $1$, we also give an algorithm whose sketch dimension, up to logarithmic factors, does not depend on $n$. It sketches the kernel plus a ridge term, and for a given $K\geq 1$ its error is at most $\epsilon\|b\|_2$ plus $(1+\sqrt{\epsilon})$ times the best residual among solutions of norm at most $(K/n)\|b\|_2$. We hope these efforts will provide an alternative perspective of studying efficient approximation of attention matrices.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song, Junze Yin, Lichen Zhang

item.title: ProFL: Performative Robust Optimal Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2410.18075v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Performative prediction is a framework that captures distribution shifts that occur during the training of machine learning models due to their deployment. As the trained model is used, the induced data distribution evolves, leading to deviations from the original data distribution. The impact of such model-induced distribution shifts in federated learning (FL) is increasingly likely to transpire in real-life use cases. A recently proposed approach extends performative prediction to FL with the resulting model converging to a performative stable point, which may be far from the performative optimal point. Earlier research in centralized settings has shown that the performative optimal point can be achieved under model-induced distribution shifts, but these approaches require the performative risk to be convex and the training data to be noiseless. These assumptions are often violated in realistic FL systems. This paper addresses these limitations and proposes Performative Robust Optimal Federated Learning (ProFL), an algorithm that targets the performative optimal point in FL while mitigating the effects of noisy and contaminated local data. We present a neighborhood-convergence analysis under the Polyak--Lojasiewicz condition, which applies to non-convex objectives. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the advantage of Robust Optimal Federated Learning over the state-of-the-art.
item.dc:creator: Xue Zheng, Tian Xie, Xuwei Tan, Xueru Zhang, Aylin Yener

item.title: Adaptive Linear Networks for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting in Big Data Systems
item.description: arXiv:2505.00590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large-scale sensing, clinical, transportation, energy, and climate systems often produce irregular multivariate time series with sparse observations, heterogeneous sampling intervals, and asynchronous variables. Forecasting at externally supplied future query coordinates requires a model to accommodate variable observation lengths and time locations while retaining efficient variable interaction. We present AiT (Adaptive inverted Transformer), whose ALinear (Adaptive Linear) module generates sample-adaptive temporal weights from observation or query coordinates. More precisely, ALinear is time-conditioned attention pooling without value projection. Available observation or query coordinates generate the corresponding keys or queries, the fixed-shape counterpart may use learned default slots, and the unprojected inputs serve as values. The name "Linear" therefore denotes only the final weighted-sum output form and not equivalence to an unrestricted affine layer or to DLinear. AiT uses ALinear to encode variable-length histories and decode query-conditioned forecasts, and applies Transformer blocks over the resulting variable tokens to model cross-variable relationships. The evaluation on four public irregular forecasting datasets examines prediction accuracy and computational efficiency, while controlled protocols are specified for temporal-design, scalability, missingness, and statistical analyses.
item.dc:creator: Chengsen Wang, Qi Qi, Bo He, Haifeng Sun, Zirui Zhuang, Jingyu Wang

item.title: Impact of Data Sparsity on Machine Learning for Fault Detection in Power System Protection
item.description: arXiv:2505.15560v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Germany's transition to a renewable energy-based power system is reshaping grid operations, requiring advanced monitoring and control to manage decentralized generation. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful tool for power system protection, particularly for fault detection (FD) and fault line identification (FLI) in transmission grids. However, ML model reliability depends on data quality and availability. Data sparsity resulting from sensor failures, communication disruptions, or reduced sampling rates poses a challenge to ML-based FD and FLI. Yet, its impact has not been systematically validated prior to this work. In response, we propose a framework to assess the impact of data sparsity on ML-based FD and FLI performance. We simulate realistic data sparsity scenarios, evaluate their impact, derive quantitative insights, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this evaluation strategy by applying it to an existing ML-based framework. After 50-fold decimation, the model achieves an F1-score of 0.999 $\pm$ 0.000 for FD. For FLI, removing current measurements reduces the F1-score by 55.61%, and the Bus 2 loss scenario reduces it by 9.73%. These results quantify the sensitivity of the two tasks to the evaluated input restrictions.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 33rd European Signal Processing Conference (EUSIPCO 2025), Palermo, Italy, Sept. 2025
item.dc:creator: Julian Oelhaf, Georg Kordowich, Changhun Kim, Paula Andrea P\'erez-Toro, Andreas Maier, Johann J\"ager, Siming Bayer

item.title: Text-to-Image Prompt Optimization for Unseen Rewards
item.description: arXiv:2506.16853v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) prompt optimization rewrites user prompts to improve the quality of generated images under a target reward. Existing methods typically assume a known reward, relying on reward-specific training or handcrafted instructions. We instead study prompt optimization for unseen rewards, which are unknown at design time and accessible only through scores at test time. We observe that removing reward-specific guidance substantially reduces the search efficiency of LLM-based optimizers, even though their optimization histories contain evidence of what the reward favors. To address this challenge, we introduce RATTPO (Reward-Adaptive Test-Time Prompt Optimization), a reward-generic method that turns this implicit evidence into explicit search guidance. At each round, RATTPO contrasts high- and low-scoring prompts to infer competing hypotheses about promising rewriting directions, then generates and evaluates candidates under each hypothesis. Across four reward families, RATTPO consistently outperforms reward-generic baselines at equal budgets and achieves performance comparable to reward-tailored optimizers without any reward-specific adjustment.
item.dc:creator: Semin Kim, Yeonwoo Cha, Jaehoon Yoo, Seunghoon Hong

item.title: On the notion of missingness for path attribution explainability methods in medical settings: Guiding the selection of medically meaningful baselines
item.description: arXiv:2508.14482v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The explainability of deep learning models remains a significant challenge, particularly in the medical domain where interpretable outputs are essential for clinical trust and transparency. Path attribution methods such as Integrated Gradients (IG) rely on a baseline that represents the absence of informative features, a notion commonly referred to as missingness. However, commonly used baselines (such as all-zero inputs) are often semantically meaningless in medical contexts, where intensity values carry clinical significance. In this work, we revisit the notion of missingness for medical imaging, expose the limitations of standard baselines in this setting, and formalize a stricter missingness we term semantic missingness: a baseline must not merely lack signal, but must represent a clinically plausible state in which the disease-related features are absent. This formulation motivates a counterfactual-guided approach to baseline selection, in which a synthetically generated counterfactual (i.e. a clinically normal variant of the pathological input) serves as a principled and semantically meaningful reference.
